title: Memory regions, allocation concepts and object lifetime
learningObjectives: Explain the concept and its C rules.
Trace the example and identify data or resource flow.
Recognize relevant safety and failure cases.
Apply the concept in a tested C program.

understand.concept: C objects have storage duration categories including automatic, static, thread and allocated storage duration. The language specifies object lifetime and storage duration, not a universal physical stack/heap layout. Dynamically allocated storage is managed through allocation functions.
understand.whyItMatters: Understanding lifetime helps determine when pointers remain valid and who is responsible for releasing allocated storage.
understand.analogy: Treat each object or stream as a resource with a defined lifetime and explicit rules for access.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace C's formal object, storage-duration, alignment or library rules.

explain.narrative:
C objects have storage duration categories including automatic, static, thread and allocated storage duration. The language specifies object lifetime and storage duration, not a universal physical stack/heap layout. Dynamically allocated storage is managed through allocation functions.

Check all allocation, I/O and conversion results. Respect object bounds and lifetime, initialize data before reading it, and define who owns and releases each resource.

examples.title: Focused C example
examples.explanation: The automatic object exists during its block execution, the static object has static storage duration, and the allocated object remains until released. The program frees the allocated storage before returning.

practise.guidedTask: Classify each object by storage duration and identify when it ceases to be valid.
practise.independentTask: Draw a lifetime timeline for a local variable, a static local and an allocated object returned from a function.
hints: Do not equate C storage-duration categories with a guaranteed physical memory layout.
Allocated storage must be released according to a clear ownership rule.
A pointer does not extend the lifetime of an automatic object.
